title: Rebalancing
desc: Bring a drifting portfolio back to its target split

cards.title: After a good year
cards.situation: Your target is 60% stocks, 40% bonds. After a strong year you have $8,000 in stocks and $3,000 in bonds. What brings you back to target?

visual.label: Target 60% stocks, 40% bonds; now 73% stocks, 27% bonds

options.feedback: Letting it run means 73% in stocks. You’re now taking more risk than you chose.
Trim what grew, top up what lagged. That’s rebalancing.
That pushes you even further from 60/40. Stocks are already above target.

cards.work: Total $11,000. 60% = $6,600 in stocks. Sell $1,400 of stocks, buy $1,400 of bonds.
cards.added: Feedback for C written for the Academy

cards.title: Drift
cards.text: Prices move, so your split slowly **drifts** away from the target. After a run-up in stocks, you hold more risk than you planned.

visual.label: The split drifts from 60/40 in January to 66/34 in June and 73/27 in December

blocks.tip: **[[rebalancing|Rebalancing]]**: bring the split back to target, once or twice a year.

cards.title: Back to 60/40
cards.text: Total $11,000. The target says $6,600 in stocks and $4,400 in bonds.

items.title: Before and after
items.label: Stocks go from $8,000 to $6,600; bonds from $3,000 to $4,400

cards.foot: You sell a bit of what rose and buy what lagged. It feels wrong, and that’s the point.

cards.title: Keep it simple
cards.text: Check the split on a set date, **once or twice a year**. Rebalance if it’s off by more than about 5 points.

blocks.tip: Each sale can cost fees, and in some accounts taxes. Rebalancing too often eats returns.

cards.title: How much to sell?
cards.q: Your target is 50% stocks, 50% bonds. Now you have $14,000 in stocks and $6,000 in bonds. How much stock do you sell?

options.feedback: Half of the whole $20,000 is $10,000. You hold $14,000, so the extra comes off.
Half of $14,000 isn’t the target. Half of the whole $20,000 is.
That only gets stocks to $12,000, still 60%. The target is half of the whole $20,000.
That sells every stock. The target is 50% stocks, not zero.

cards.title: How often?
cards.q: How often does a typical long-term investor rebalance?

options.feedback: Daily rebalancing piles up costs and chases noise. Once or twice a year keeps the split close enough.
Once or twice a year keeps the split close enough without piling up costs.
Without rebalancing the split keeps drifting, and your risk drifts with it.
Drift comes from good years too. A set date, once or twice a year, catches both.
